title: Asking What the Customer Wants
subtitle: How to ask the right questions before you recommend anything
description: Learn the words and phrases sales professionals use to discover what a customer really needs — from asking about problems and priorities to finding the right fit and recommending a solution.
dialogueSubtitle: Riley follows up with Dana to understand what she really needs before making a recommendation

vocabulary.definition: To suggest something as the best choice for someone.
vocabulary.example: Before I recommend a plan, I need to understand what you're looking for.

vocabulary.definition: A situation that causes difficulty or needs to be fixed.
vocabulary.example: Our main problem is that our tools don't connect with each other.

vocabulary.definition: The thing that is most important and needs attention first.
vocabulary.example: What's your top priority right now — saving time or cutting costs?

vocabulary.definition: Something you want to achieve or reach.
vocabulary.example: Our goal is to get better visibility into what the team is working on.

vocabulary.definition: The right match for someone's needs or situation.
vocabulary.example: It's a great fit for teams that want something powerful but easy to learn.
What option would you suggest for a team of about twelve people?

vocabulary.definition: To require something — it is necessary or very important.
vocabulary.example: We need a tool that is simple enough for everyone on the team to use.

vocabulary.definition: An answer or fix to a problem.
vocabulary.example: Is there a solution for teams that already use three different apps?

phrasalVerbs.definition: Ask a customer what they want or need — the key opening question in any needs discovery conversation.
phrasalVerbs.example: Before I show you anything, what are you looking for in a project management tool?

phrasalVerbs.definition: Find out what the customer considers most important.
phrasalVerbs.example: What's your main priority right now — saving time, cutting costs, or better collaboration?

phrasalVerbs.phrase: WHAT WOULD MAKE THIS A SUCCESS FOR YOU
phrasalVerbs.definition: Ask the customer how they would know if the product or service was working.
phrasalVerbs.example: What would make this a success for you six months from now?

phrasalVerbs.definition: Find out what solutions the customer has already tried and what didn't work.
phrasalVerbs.example: Have you tried anything before, or is this the first time you're looking at this kind of tool?

phrasalVerbs.phrase: BASED ON WHAT YOU'VE TOLD ME
phrasalVerbs.definition: Use this to transition from listening to recommending — show you were paying attention.
phrasalVerbs.example: Based on what you've told me, I'd suggest the Growth Plan.

phrasalVerbs.definition: Check whether your suggestion fits the customer's needs before moving forward.
phrasalVerbs.example: The starter plan covers everything you mentioned — would that work for you?

dialogue.speaker: Riley
dialogue.text: Thanks for making time, Dana. Before I [[recommend:to suggest something as the best choice for someone]] a plan, I want to make sure I understand what you're looking for.

dialogue.speaker: Dana
dialogue.text: Of course. Right now our main [[problem:a situation that causes difficulty or needs to be fixed]] is that our team uses five different tools and nothing connects.

dialogue.speaker: Riley
dialogue.text: I hear that a lot. What is your top [[priority:the thing that is most important and needs attention first]] — saving time, cutting costs, or making it easier to work together?

dialogue.speaker: Dana
dialogue.text: Saving time, for sure. We waste hours every week just trying to track what everyone is doing.

dialogue.speaker: Riley
dialogue.text: So your main [[goal:something you want to achieve or reach]] is better visibility into what your team is working on?

dialogue.speaker: Dana
dialogue.text: Exactly. And whatever we choose needs to be simple — that's non-negotiable for us.

dialogue.speaker: Riley
dialogue.text: That's where Brightline stands out. It's a great [[fit:the right match for someone's needs or situation]] for teams that want something powerful but easy to learn.

dialogue.speaker: Dana
dialogue.text: Good to hear. What [[option:one of the choices available]] would you suggest for a team of about twelve people?

dialogue.speaker: Riley
dialogue.text: I'd suggest the Growth Plan — it has everything you [[need:to require something that is necessary]] without the extra features you'd never use.

dialogue.speaker: Dana
dialogue.text: And is there a [[solution:an answer or fix to a problem]] for the fact that we currently use three different apps for tracking?

dialogue.speaker: Riley
dialogue.text: Yes — Brightline connects with most of the tools you're already using, so you don't have to give anything up.

dialogue.speaker: Dana
dialogue.text: That's exactly what we needed to hear. Let's move forward.

chooseResponse.instructions: Work in groups. Read the customer's line, then discuss which response (A, B, or C) is best. Choose your answer together, then click to see if you were right — and why.

items.customerLine: I'm not sure what I need — we have a few different problems.
options: Don't worry — I'll just recommend our most popular plan.
That's a great place to start. What would you say is the biggest problem right now?
I'll send you information about all our options and you can decide.
items.explanation: B is correct. Asking for the biggest problem narrows the focus, which is exactly how good needs discovery works. A skips the discovery entirely and recommends without understanding. C delays the conversation instead of helping right now.

items.customerLine: What would you recommend for a team our size?
options: Before I recommend anything, can I ask — what's your main priority right now?
I recommend the Growth Plan — most companies your size choose that one.
It depends. What's your budget?
items.explanation: A is correct. Asking about priority before recommending shows you want the right fit, not just a quick sale. B recommends without understanding the customer's specific needs or goals. C is on the right track but asking about budget before priority skips an important step.

items.customerLine: We tried something similar before and it didn't work out.
options: Oh, that's a shame. Our product is a lot better than most.
I'm sorry to hear that. What didn't work — was it the features, the fit with your team, or something else?
Most tools have that problem. Ours is different, I promise.
items.explanation: B is correct. It shows empathy and asks a specific follow-up to understand what went wrong — which is valuable information for finding the right solution. A is dismissive. C is vague and sounds like an empty promise.

items.customerLine: We already have a solution for that.
options: Then maybe our product isn't what you're looking for.
Are you sure? Our solution is probably a better fit.
Great — is it meeting all your needs, or is there something it doesn't do that you'd love to have?
items.explanation: C is correct. It acknowledges their current solution and gently opens the door to an unmet need. A gives up far too early. B sounds argumentative and dismissive of what the customer already has.

profileMatch.instructions: Good discovery starts with the right type of question. Read each customer situation and decide which question approach is best — open and broad, problem-focused, or timeline-focused. Use phrases from this lesson to justify your choices. Click 'Check Matches' when you agree.

profiles.name: Omar
profiles.description: Omar is a marketing director who was referred to Brightline by a colleague. He hasn't thought much about the specific problems he wants to solve — he's just curious. He's open to the conversation.

profiles.name: Sarah
profiles.description: Sarah emailed to say her team 'keeps missing deadlines and losing track of client feedback.' She knows exactly what her pain is. She wants to feel understood before she hears about any product.

profiles.name: James
profiles.description: James mentioned that his company is switching tools 'before the end of Q3.' He has a deadline and needs to move quickly. He doesn't have time for a long discovery process.

options.label: Open, broad questions
options.description: Start wide: 'Tell me about how your team currently works.' or 'What would better look like for you?' Good for contacts who are still exploring and haven't defined a problem yet.

options.label: Problem-focused questions
options.description: Go straight to the pain: 'What is the biggest challenge you are trying to fix?' or 'How is that affecting the team?' Good when the customer has already named a problem and wants to feel heard.

options.label: Timeline-focused questions
options.description: Focus on urgency and next steps: 'When do you need this in place?' or 'What happens if you don't have a solution by then?' Good for contacts who are already decided and moving fast.

finishTheLine.instructions: The salesperson's line has been cut off. As a group, discuss how you would finish it. Try to use vocabulary from this lesson. There is no single correct answer — compare your ideas, then click to see one possible answer.
